title: A Better Room for an Old Enzyme
paragraphs: Every leaf on Earth depends on an enzyme that is, by the standards of its profession, both slow and careless.
Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase, mercifully shortened to rubisco, attaches carbon dioxide from the air to a five-carbon sugar in the chloroplast.
The product splits at once into two molecules of a three-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglycerate, which is why the ordinary pathway of carbon fixation is called C3 photosynthesis.

Rubisco manages only a few reactions per second, a sluggish pace for an enzyme, and plants compensate by making enormous amounts of it; it is generally thought to be the most abundant protein on the planet.
Slowness is a nuisance; the carelessness is worse.
Rubisco cannot reliably tell carbon dioxide from oxygen, and when an oxygen molecule arrives instead, it attaches that to the same sugar.
That reaction, the oxygenase half of the name, yields one useful 3-phosphoglycerate and one two-carbon compound, phosphoglycolate, which the Calvin cycle cannot use.
Salvaging that carbon takes a roundabout route through the chloroplast, the peroxisome, and the mitochondrion, costs energy, and returns some carbon to the air.
Botanists call the whole wasteful detour photorespiration, because a leaf running it consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide in the light, as if it were breathing.
On a hot, bright day photorespiration can undo a quarter or more of what a C3 leaf has fixed.
It is natural to ask why natural selection has tolerated such a flaw for so long, and the likeliest answer is history.
Rubisco arose in microbes more than two billion years ago, in air rich in carbon dioxide and nearly empty of oxygen, so there was no rival gas to discriminate against.
By the time photosynthesis had filled the air with oxygen the design was set.
The flaw bites hardest when a plant can least afford it: heat lowers rubisco's preference for carbon dioxide, and warm water holds less dissolved carbon dioxide relative to oxygen.

Drought makes matters worse, because a leaf conserves water by closing its stomata, the pores on its surface, and a closed leaf runs down its internal carbon dioxide while photosynthesis keeps generating oxygen.
A C3 plant in a hot, dry field is therefore trapped: open the stomata and lose water, or close them and feed rubisco the wrong gas.
The way out was found, fittingly, in a crop that thrives in those conditions.

In 1965 Hugo Kortschak and colleagues at a sugar research station in Hawaii reported that when sugarcane leaves were fed radioactive carbon dioxide, the label appeared first not in 3-phosphoglycerate but in the four-carbon acids malate and aspartate.

The next year Marshall Hatch and Roger Slack, biochemists in the Australian sugar industry, confirmed the finding and traced the carbon from those acids into the ordinary Calvin cycle, showing that sugarcane ran a second carboxylation in front of rubisco.
It is now called C4 photosynthesis, after the carbons in its first product, though for years it was simply the Hatch-Slack pathway.

The chemistry depends on a second enzyme, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, or PEP carboxylase, which attaches carbon to a three-carbon acceptor, phosphoenolpyruvate, to make four-carbon oxaloacetate, quickly converted to malate.
Two properties make PEP carboxylase an ideal front end for rubisco.

First, it takes its carbon not as dissolved gas but as bicarbonate ion, which the leaf's carbonic anhydrase makes from carbon dioxide almost instantly, so it gathers carbon even when little is present.
Second, it has no oxygenase activity at all; oxygen simply does not fit.
The four-carbon acid is a parcel, and its job is delivery.

The delivery requires a floor plan that the botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt had described in the 1880s, decades before anyone understood it: in certain grasses the cells around each leaf vein form a conspicuous ring, which he called Kranz anatomy, German for wreath.

In a C4 leaf the outer cells of the wreath, the mesophyll, hold PEP carboxylase but no rubisco; the inner ring of bundle sheath cells, pressed against the vein, holds rubisco and the Calvin cycle, often behind thickened walls that resist the leakage of gas.
Malate made in the mesophyll diffuses through channels into the bundle sheath, where an enzyme strips off its carbon dioxide and hands the gas to rubisco.

Because parcels keep arriving and the gas cannot easily escape, carbon dioxide in the bundle sheath climbs to several times its level in an ordinary leaf, and there rubisco almost never mistakes oxygen for its substrate.
The three-carbon leftover, pyruvate, returns to the mesophyll to be rebuilt into phosphoenolpyruvate.
The pump is not free.
Rebuilding phosphoenolpyruvate costs roughly two extra ATP for every carbon dioxide delivered, so a C4 leaf spends about five ATP per carbon fixed where a C3 leaf spends three.
In cool, dim, or humid conditions, where rubisco's confusion is mild, that surcharge outweighs the savings and C3 plants win; in heat and strong light the balance tips the other way.
The distribution of C4 plants follows that arithmetic.

They are only about three percent of flowering plant species, yet they include maize, sugarcane, sorghum, and millet, dominate the tropical grasslands, and account for roughly a quarter of the primary productivity on land.
Most are grasses, but not all: amaranths and some saltbushes use the trick, and the pathway has evolved independently more than sixty times.
A few desert plants of Central Asia even run the whole cycle inside single cells, with no wreath at all, which shows that the anatomy serves the chemistry rather than the reverse.
Succulents solved the same problem with the same enzyme and a different arrangement: they separate the two carboxylations in time rather than in space.
The pattern is called crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, after the stonecrop family, and it occurs in cacti, agaves, pineapple, and many orchids.
A CAM plant opens its stomata at night, when the air is cool and an open pore costs the least water.
PEP carboxylase fixes the carbon dioxide that enters into malate, which the plant stores as malic acid in the large vacuoles of its cells.
By dawn the tissue is markedly sour.
Then the stomata close for the day, the stored acid is broken down, and the released carbon dioxide reaches rubisco behind sealed pores, in the daylight the Calvin cycle needs.
The sourness had been noticed long before the chemistry.

In 1815 Benjamin Heyne, a physician in India, reported to the Linnean Society of London that the leaves of a succulent tasted as acid as sorrel in the morning and lost the taste as the day wore on, a rhythm he could not explain.
What the rhythm buys is water: a C3 crop commonly transpires several hundred grams of water per gram of carbon dioxide fixed, and a CAM plant manages on a small fraction of that.
The price is speed, since a night's worth of stored acid is a small ration of carbon, and CAM plants are among the slowest growers in the plant kingdom.
The textbook summary, that C4 answers heat and CAM answers drought, is tidy, and I think slightly too tidy.
Some quillworts, small plants rooted in shallow ponds, run CAM entirely underwater, where no water is being conserved.

There the nighttime uptake serves a different shortage: by day the pond's other plants strip the water of carbon dioxide, and only at night does the supply recover, so the quillwort gathers carbon when it can and spends it later.
What CAM and C4 share is not a climate but a strategy, which is to keep rubisco away from the open air and feed it from a concentrated store.

Rice, a staple for about half of humanity, is a C3 plant, and since 2008 an international consortium has been trying to install the C4 pathway in it, one of the most ambitious projects in plant science.
I admire the ambition, and I doubt the timetable.

Moving a pathway means moving not just a handful of enzymes but a floor plan, a set of cell-specific switches, and a transport system, and each of the sixty-odd natural inventions of C4 took a very long time.
Still, rubisco's lesson is worth remembering whenever we are tempted to call a piece of biology badly designed.
The enzyme is not broken; it is old, and plants have twice found ways to build a better room around it rather than a better worker.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the ordinary pathway of carbon fixation is called C3 photosynthesis because
choices: rubisco attaches carbon dioxide to a three-carbon sugar inside the chloroplast
the enzyme completes only about three reactions per second
its first product is a three-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglycerate
three organelles cooperate to salvage the carbon that rubisco misplaces
the pathway was the third form of photosynthesis to be discovered

proof.quote: two molecules of a three-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglycerate, which is why the ordinary pathway of carbon fixation is called C3 photosynthesis

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the product splits into two molecules of a three-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglycerate, and that this is why the ordinary pathway is called C3 photosynthesis. The name comes from the first product.
distractorNotes: Wrong detail: paragraph 1 says the acceptor sugar has five carbons, not three.
Outside the passage: paragraph 1 says only a few reactions per second and never ties the name to that pace.
Wrong paragraph: the three organelles in paragraph 2 belong to photorespiration, not to the pathway's name.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the order in which pathways were discovered.

questions.stem: According to the passage, photorespiration gets its name from the fact that
choices: the salvage route passes through the mitochondrion, the organelle of respiration
rubisco attaches oxygen rather than carbon dioxide to its five-carbon sugar
the detour costs the leaf energy, much as breathing costs an animal
phosphoglycolate is broken down only at night, when the leaf is not photosynthesizing
the leaf consumes oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide while in the light

proof.quote: because a leaf running it consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide in the light, as if it were breathing

questions.why: Paragraph 2 explains the name directly: a leaf running the detour consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide in the light, as if it were breathing.
distractorNotes: Half right: the mitochondrion is on the salvage route in paragraph 2, but the passage never ties the name to it.
Wrong step: that is the oxygenase reaction that starts the problem, not the reason given for the name.
Wrong reason: the energy cost is real, but paragraph 2 names the gas exchange, not the cost, as the source of the name.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the exchange happens in the light; nothing says the breakdown waits for night.

questions.stem: The author mentions the atmosphere of more than two billion years ago in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: show that rubisco was once a faster enzyme than it is today
explain why a flawed enzyme could persist despite natural selection
argue that oxygen entered the atmosphere more recently than carbon dioxide did
establish that microbes rather than plants were the first organisms to use rubisco
prove that heat and drought were common on the early Earth

proof.quote: why natural selection has tolerated such a flaw for so long, and the likeliest answer is history
so there was no rival gas to discriminate against

questions.why: Paragraph 3 opens by asking why selection tolerated the flaw and answers with history. The ancient atmosphere is the evidence: with no oxygen around, there was no rival gas to discriminate against, so the design was set before the flaw mattered.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing says rubisco was ever faster than it is now.
Half right: the passage implies oxygen came later, but as support for the point about history, not as the point itself.
Wrong emphasis: microbes are mentioned in passing; the paragraph's question is why the flaw survived.
Wrong detail: heat and drought appear later in the paragraph as present-day conditions, not ancient ones.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a C3 plant that closes its stomata during a hot afternoon will most likely
choices: stop producing oxygen until the pores reopen
lose more water than a neighboring plant whose stomata stay open
shift its carbon fixation to PEP carboxylase
see photorespiration rise as its internal carbon dioxide falls
fix carbon more quickly because it is no longer losing water

proof.quote: a closed leaf runs down its internal carbon dioxide while photosynthesis keeps generating oxygen
close them and feed rubisco the wrong gas

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says a closed leaf runs down its internal carbon dioxide while oxygen keeps building, which means feeding rubisco the wrong gas. Paragraph 2 told us what that produces: the oxygenase reaction and photorespiration.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 3 says photosynthesis keeps generating oxygen behind closed pores.
Reversed: closing the stomata is how the leaf conserves water, so it loses less, not more.
Outside the passage: PEP carboxylase belongs to C4 and CAM plants, not to a C3 plant.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the closed leaf feeds rubisco the wrong gas, the opposite of faster fixation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hatch and Slack
choices: traced carbon from four-carbon acids into the Calvin cycle
were the first to report that radioactive carbon appeared in malate and aspartate
worked at a sugar planters' research station in Hawaii
named the pathway C4 photosynthesis after its first product
discovered the enzyme PEP carboxylase in maize leaves

proof.quote: traced the carbon from those acids into the ordinary Calvin cycle

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says Hatch and Slack confirmed the Hawaiian finding and traced the carbon from the four-carbon acids into the ordinary Calvin cycle, showing a second carboxylation in front of rubisco.
distractorNotes: Wrong team: paragraph 4 credits the first report, in 1965, to Kortschak's group in Hawaii.
Wrong place: Hatch and Slack worked in the Australian sugar industry; the Hawaiian station was Kortschak's.
Outside the passage: paragraph 4 says what the pathway is now called but never says who named it.
Outside the passage: nothing says they discovered the enzyme, and their plant was sugarcane, not maize.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one reason PEP carboxylase works well as a front end for rubisco is that it
choices: runs several times faster than rubisco at the same temperature
operates only in the bundle sheath, where oxygen is scarce
converts carbon dioxide into bicarbonate ion on its own
has no oxygenase activity, since oxygen does not fit it
releases its carbon directly into the Calvin cycle without a carrier

proof.quote: it has no oxygenase activity at all; oxygen simply does not fit

questions.why: Paragraph 5 lists two properties, and the second is stated plainly: PEP carboxylase has no oxygenase activity at all, because oxygen simply does not fit.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the passage never compares the speeds of the two enzymes.
Wrong cell: paragraph 6 places PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll, the outer ring, not the bundle sheath.
Half right: it uses bicarbonate, but paragraph 5 says carbonic anhydrase makes the bicarbonate, not PEP carboxylase.
Contradicted: paragraph 5 says its product is a parcel whose job is delivery, carried to rubisco rather than released directly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true of the bundle sheath cells of a C4 leaf EXCEPT:
choices: They hold rubisco and the Calvin cycle.
They contain PEP carboxylase but no rubisco.
They are pressed against the leaf vein.
They receive malate that diffuses in from the mesophyll.
They are often wrapped in thickened walls.

proof.quote: holds rubisco and the Calvin cycle
pressed against the vein
Malate made in the mesophyll diffuses through channels into the bundle sheath
often behind thickened walls that resist the leakage of gas
the mesophyll, hold PEP carboxylase but no rubisco

questions.why: Paragraph 6 assigns PEP carboxylase, and no rubisco, to the outer mesophyll cells. The bundle sheath is the inner ring that holds rubisco and the Calvin cycle; the other four statements all come from paragraph 6.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 6, sentence 2 says the bundle sheath holds rubisco and the Calvin cycle.
Paragraph 6, sentence 2 says the inner ring is pressed against the vein.
Paragraph 6, sentence 3 says malate made in the mesophyll diffuses into the bundle sheath.
Paragraph 6, sentence 2 says the Calvin cycle sits behind thickened walls that resist leakage.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'arithmetic' most nearly means
choices: a weighing of costs against benefits
the branch of mathematics dealing with numbers
a count of the species in a family
a sum computed by adding figures together
an exact measurement taken in the field

proof.quote: The distribution of C4 plants follows that arithmetic.
that surcharge outweighs the savings and C3 plants win; in heat and strong light the balance tips the other way

questions.why: The sentence before explains a surcharge weighed against savings, with the balance tipping one way in cool conditions and the other in heat. The arithmetic that C4 distribution follows is that cost-against-benefit comparison.
distractorNotes: The everyday meaning; no computation with numbers is being performed in the sentence.
Wrong referent: the species figure comes after this sentence as a consequence, not as what the word refers to.
Too literal: the sentence points back to a comparison of cost and savings, not to an addition problem.
Outside the passage: no measurement is described; the word refers to the reasoning of the previous sentence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, C4 plants
choices: make up about a quarter of all flowering plant species on Earth
are almost entirely limited to members of the grass family
account for about three percent of the primary productivity on land
include rice, maize, and sorghum among their number
dominate the tropical grasslands despite being few in species

proof.quote: They are only about three percent of flowering plant species, yet they include maize, sugarcane, sorghum, and millet, dominate the tropical grasslands

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says C4 plants are only about three percent of flowering plant species, yet they dominate the tropical grasslands and account for roughly a quarter of productivity on land.
distractorNotes: Swapped numbers: a quarter is their share of productivity, not of species.
Too strong: paragraph 7 says most are grasses but names amaranths and saltbushes as well.
Swapped numbers: three percent is their share of species; their share of productivity is about a quarter.
Wrong plant: paragraph 11 says rice is a C3 plant.

questions.stem: The author mentions the desert plants of Central Asia in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: show that C4 photosynthesis can evolve even in plants that are not grasses
introduce the succulents that will be discussed in the next paragraph
show that the anatomy serves the chemistry rather than the reverse
argue that the C4 pathway first arose in deserts and only later spread to grasslands
illustrate how many separate times the pathway has arisen

proof.quote: which shows that the anatomy serves the chemistry rather than the reverse

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says these plants run the whole cycle inside single cells with no wreath at all, and spells out the point: the anatomy serves the chemistry rather than the reverse.
distractorNotes: Wrong detail: the non-grass point is made with amaranths and saltbushes in the sentence before.
Wrong link: the succulents of paragraph 8 are introduced on their own and are not these desert plants.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about where the pathway first arose.
Wrong detail: the count of more than sixty origins is a separate point in the previous sentence.

questions.stem: A farmer must choose between a C3 grass and a C4 grass for a pasture in a cool, cloudy, humid valley. Based on the reasoning in paragraph 7, the passage would predict that
choices: the C4 grass will outgrow the C3 grass because its pump never shuts off
the two grasses will grow equally well, because that climate removes rubisco's flaw entirely
the C4 grass will do better only if the valley also suffers from drought
the C4 grass will switch to the C3 pathway once the surcharge becomes too high
the C3 grass will do better, since the surcharge outweighs its savings there

proof.quote: In cool, dim, or humid conditions, where rubisco's confusion is mild, that surcharge outweighs the savings and C3 plants win

questions.why: Paragraph 7 gives the rule: in cool, dim, or humid conditions rubisco's confusion is mild, so the C4 surcharge outweighs the savings and C3 plants win. A cool, cloudy, humid valley is exactly that case.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 7 says the C4 surcharge is a cost that pays off only in heat and strong light.
Too strong: paragraph 7 says rubisco's confusion is mild in such conditions, not absent, and still names a winner.
Wrong rule: paragraph 7 ties the C4 advantage to heat and strong light, and drought is not part of the stated rule.
Outside the passage: nothing in the passage describes a plant trading one pathway for the other.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the leaves of a CAM plant would taste
choices: sour at dusk and bland at dawn
most sour at dawn and less sour by the end of the day
equally sour at every hour, since acid is stored permanently
sour only during a drought, when the stomata stay closed
sweet in the morning, once the stored malate has become sugar

proof.quote: By dawn the tissue is markedly sour.
Then the stomata close for the day, the stored acid is broken down

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the acid is stored through the night, so by dawn the tissue is markedly sour, and then the stored acid is broken down during the day. Sourness peaks at dawn and fades by evening.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 8 says the acid builds overnight and is broken down by day.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the stored acid is broken down during the day.
Outside the passage: the night-and-day rhythm is routine for a CAM plant, not a drought response.
Outside the passage: nothing says the malate becomes sugar or that the leaf turns sweet.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Benjamin Heyne
choices: worked out the chemistry behind the daily change in taste
was the first to study the stonecrop family closely
measured how much water a succulent lost at night
reported a daily change in a succulent's taste
showed that quillworts take up carbon dioxide at night

proof.quote: the leaves of a succulent tasted as acid as sorrel in the morning and lost the taste as the day wore on

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says Heyne reported in 1815 that a succulent's leaves tasted as acid as sorrel in the morning and lost the taste as the day wore on, a rhythm he could not explain.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 9 says the rhythm was one he could not explain.
Outside the passage: the stonecrop family is mentioned in paragraph 8 without any researcher attached.
Outside the passage: the water figures in paragraph 9 are not attributed to Heyne.
Wrong detail: the quillworts in paragraph 10 are described with no researcher named.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of CAM plants EXCEPT:
choices: They grow faster than most C3 plants do.
They open their stomata during the night.
They store malic acid in large vacuoles.
They include cacti, agaves, and pineapple.
They fix carbon dioxide using PEP carboxylase.

proof.quote: A CAM plant opens its stomata at night
stores as malic acid in the large vacuoles
cacti, agaves, pineapple
PEP carboxylase fixes the carbon dioxide
CAM plants are among the slowest growers in the plant kingdom

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the price of CAM is speed and that CAM plants are among the slowest growers in the plant kingdom. The other four statements all come from paragraph 8.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8, sentence 3 says a CAM plant opens its stomata at night.
Paragraph 8, sentence 4 says the malate is stored as malic acid in large vacuoles.
Paragraph 8, sentence 2 lists cacti, agaves, and pineapple among CAM plants.
Paragraph 8, sentence 4 says PEP carboxylase fixes the carbon dioxide that enters.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the carbon dioxide dissolved in a shallow pond inhabited by quillworts is most likely
choices: constant throughout the day, because the quillworts keep it in balance
highest in the afternoon, when the pond's plants are most active
unaffected by the plants rooted in the pond
lowest at the end of the day and highest late at night
depleted at night, when the quillworts take it up

proof.quote: by day the pond's other plants strip the water of carbon dioxide, and only at night does the supply recover

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the pond's other plants strip the water of carbon dioxide by day and the supply recovers only at night. So the supply is at its lowest when the day ends and at its highest after a night of recovery.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 describes a daily fall and recovery in the supply.
Reversed: the plants' daytime activity strips the water of carbon dioxide rather than adding to it.
Contradicted: the pond's other plants are exactly what deplete it by day.
Half right: the quillwort does take it up at night, but paragraph 10 says night is when the supply recovers.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the project to install the C4 pathway in rice is best described as
choices: openly dismissive
admiring but doubtful
unreservedly enthusiastic
largely indifferent
deeply alarmed

proof.quote: I admire the ambition, and I doubt the timetable.
each of the sixty-odd natural inventions of C4 took a very long time

questions.why: Paragraph 11 states it in one line: the author admires the ambition and doubts the timetable, then lists why moving a pathway is hard. Admiration plus doubt is the whole attitude.
distractorNotes: Too negative: the author says plainly that the ambition is admirable.
Too positive: the author doubts the timetable and lists the obstacles.
Wrong register: the author takes a clear position on both the aim and the schedule.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 11 expresses fear or warning about the project.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Rubisco is the slowest and least accurate enzyme in the plant kingdom, and photorespiration is the price of that failing
C4 and CAM plants have replaced rubisco with PEP carboxylase, an enzyme that cannot mistake oxygen for carbon dioxide
Plants have twice evolved ways of feeding rubisco concentrated carbon dioxide rather than replacing the flawed enzyme itself
Because C4 plants dominate the tropics and account for a quarter of land productivity, engineering the pathway into rice should be straightforward
The discovery of C4 photosynthesis in sugarcane during the 1960s overturned the long-held belief that all plants fix carbon the same way

proof.quote: Succulents solved the same problem with the same enzyme and a different arrangement
What CAM and C4 share is not a climate but a strategy, which is to keep rubisco away from the open air and feed it from a concentrated store
plants have twice found ways to build a better room around it rather than a better worker

questions.why: The passage sets up rubisco's flaw, then shows C4 and CAM as two arrangements that feed the same enzyme from a concentrated store, and closes by saying plants built a better room around the enzyme rather than a better worker. The answer covers both halves.
distractorNotes: Too narrow and too strong: the flaw is only the setup, and the passage never ranks rubisco against every enzyme.
Contradicted: PEP carboxylase is a front end that delivers carbon to rubisco; paragraph 6 says rubisco still does the fixing.
Reversed: paragraph 11 doubts the timetable and lists why moving the pathway is hard.
Too narrow: the discovery is one episode in paragraph 4, and the passage never mentions such a belief.
